state.misconception_label: Does not understand that 2n represents an even number

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: Which of these shows part of the proof that the sum of two odd numbers is even? I got \( \begin{array}{l}2 n+(2 m+1) \\ =2(n+m)+1\end{array} \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have a bag of marbles. If you have 2 bags, each containing n marbles, you would have a total of 2n marbles. Similarly, if you have 2 odd numbers, the sum will always be even because they can be paired up. So, 2n represents an even number in this context.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I get that 2n means you have an even number because it's like having pairs of marbles. But when I added 2n and 2m+1, I thought it would still be odd because of the +1 part. So, does that mean I should always think of 2n as even, no matter what I add to it?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have two sets of friends, one with an even number of friends and one with an odd number of friends. When you combine the two groups, the total number of friends will always be even, even if you add one more friend. So, yes, you should always think of 2n as representing an even number, no matter what you add to it.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: So, if I get it right, 2n is always even, but when I add something odd like 2m+1, it makes the whole thing odd? I’m still a bit confused about how that works. Can you explain again how adding an odd number changes the total?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher addresses the misconception that 2n is even but uses confusing analogies and provides mathematically incorrect statements (Turn 3 claims adding odd to even gives even), while the student shows increasing confusion rather than improvement, ending more uncertain than they began.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete real-world analogies (bags of marbles, groups of friends) to explain abstract algebraic concepts, though the analogies in Turn 3 are somewhat imprecise regarding the mathematical claim being proven.
